newsitem.title: INDIA: YEAREND - Price falls may fuel India's gold hunger.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Price falls may fuel India's gold hunger.

text.p: A downtrend in global gold prices could further fuel India's hunger for the precious metal in 1997, reinforcing the country's standing as the world's largest consumer, dealers and and analysts said.
"I expect world gold prices to move in the range of US$355-$385 an ounce through next year compared to $360-$400 in 1996," said Makhan Lal Damani, president of the Bombay Bullion Association.
"More imports are expected if prices continue to rule low," Damani told Reuters.
Indian gold prices have moved in the range of 5,000-5,600 rupees per 10 grammes in the last one year, their ups and downs determined by world trends.

Analysts say India's affinity with gold has turned it into the world's largest consumer of the metal, although nearly a third of its 900 million people live below the poverty line, with the average per capita income at around $330 a year.
India's annual consumption of gold is estimated at around 500 tonnes, most of it imported. Official figures put the cost of gold imports in 1995 at $3.4 billion -- second only to oil in value.
For all its insatiable appetite for gold, India's production has been insignificant. Its domestic output from the Kolar mines in the south is woefully low at two tonnes a year.

India lifted a ban on gold imports in 1990 and gradually liberalised gold trade, allowing expatriate Indians to bring up to five kgs into the country once every six months, subject to a duty of 220 rupees per 10 grammes.
WEDDING JEWLLERY DEMAND DRIVES GOLD SALES
India's main demand for gold is in jewellery for the estimated 10 million wedding ceremonies each year, which absorb nearly 300 tonnes of the metal, bullion dealers said.
India's wedding season, beginning in November and lasting up to February, is currently in full swing.

"There are so many weddings in a single day that I had to rush from one to another at breakneck speed," said jeweller Ajit Jain. He said imports of gold would rise because of India's population growth and the role th emetal played in people's lives.
"Wedding ceremonies and religious functions are there in larger numbers than before. The volumes are big, though quantities bought for each occasion are dwindling," Jain said.
Gold is looked upon as security by people in rural areas, where 70 percent of the population lives. It is also used as a hedge against inflation.
"Investment buying in gold has been declining," Jain said. "India's consumer goods' revolution, spread through television advertising, has left people with less money to buy gold."
INDIA HOLDS SEVEN PERCENT OF TOTAL WORLD GOLD STOCKS

India's gold holdings are put at around 9,000 tonnes, accumulated from centuries of trading and account for about seven percent of an estimated world stock of 128,000 tonnes. These holdings mainly comprise family heirlooms and jewels given as part of dowries at weddings.
Top officials of the World Gold Council (WGC), who attended a seminar on gold in New Delhi in November, said India could use its dormant gold resources to develop a jewellery export sector.
"There is no reason, given India's infrastructure and its skills, why it should not be a major player in the gold export markets," WGC chief executive Elliot Hood told Reuters.
WGC economist George Milling-Stanley said developing countries, including India, were accounting for higher demand every year compared to their developed counterparts.
"This is partly because of thousands of years of affinity with gold. There is a real understanding of the value of gold in this part of the world," he said.
Indian government officials, who addressed the seminar, promised to further liberalise gold imports and reduce customs duty on the metal.
"We are expecting some reduction in customs duty on gold, which would result in higher imports," said Jain.
Analysts said they believed India had the potential to step up its per capita gold consumption to one gramme (0.04 ounces) from the present 0.5 grammes (0.02 ounces).
"This would amount to a total consumption of 1,000 tonnes a year in the near future," said one. "It's mind-boggling."
A package of economic reforms, initiated in 1991, has vested India's estimated 200-million strong middle class with growing purchasing power.
"A part of the middle-class income will always come into gold," the analyst added.
